title: The Role of Family and Friends in Shaping Your Habits
coreMove: Pick the specific group whose normal behavior you want to inherit, then arrange your week so you are inside it often enough for its defaults to become yours.

exampleSpecs.domain: a hospice nurse who keeps slipping back into smoking on night shifts because the only people who take breaks with her are the two smokers on her unit
exampleSpecs.audience: a shift worker whose social options at work are narrow and fixed
exampleSpecs.stakes: a quit attempt she has restarted four times in two years
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she names the smoke-break duo as her real reference group at 3am, not the non-smoking friends she sees on Saturdays, and reshuffles who she takes her ten-minute break with

exampleSpecs.domain: a couple disagreeing about whether to join a Sunday cycling club that meets at 6am
exampleSpecs.audience: a partnered adult negotiating a habit that pulls them away from a shared household
exampleSpecs.stakes: one of them wants to ride with stronger riders to become one; the other reads the early start as the marriage losing
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the rider articulates that the point is to spend Sunday mornings as someone for whom 6am rides are ordinary, and the partner counters with what gets normalized in her week instead

exampleSpecs.domain: a thirteen-year-old quietly dropping a reading habit after switching lunch tables to sit with a louder group
exampleSpecs.audience: a parent watching a child's peer group shift mid-school-year
exampleSpecs.stakes: a kid who used to finish a novel a week is now finishing none, and the parent has noticed but not named it
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the parent sees that the new table, not the phone or the homework load, is doing the work — and resists the instinct to ban the friends, choosing instead to seed a second group around the old habit

exampleSpecs.domain: a line cook trying to eat home-cooked meals on his days off while living with three roommates who order delivery five nights a week
exampleSpecs.audience: a young adult in a shared household with mismatched habits
exampleSpecs.stakes: his food costs and his energy on doubles, both quietly eroding
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he chooses between moving out, converting the roommates, or finding a third group (a Sunday meal-prep crew two blocks away) to be the tribe that normalizes cooking — and picks the third

exampleSpecs.domain: a regional sales manager who notices her quarterly numbers track almost exactly with which two colleagues she eats lunch with
exampleSpecs.audience: a mid-career professional inside a large, mixed-performance team
exampleSpecs.stakes: a promotion cycle six months out and a habit of coasting at lunch with the steadiest underperformers
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: before seeing the numbers laid out, she predicts which lunch-group quarters were her strongest; the reveal lines up, and she has to decide whether to switch tables knowing exactly what it will cost socially

exampleSpecs.domain: a recently sober electrician whose entire weekend social life was built around one specific bar
exampleSpecs.audience: an adult in early recovery whose old tribe is the cue
exampleSpecs.stakes: eight months sober, a wedding coming up where the old crew will be, and Saturdays that currently have nothing in them
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he works through which of his old friendships were about the person and which were about the room, and commits to two specific Saturday formats (a 7am gym class, a Sunday-prep barbecue with two coworkers) before the wedding, not after
